podcast.title: Decca Session Musician (1956)
podcast.body: Grady Martin was one of the regular session musicians Owen Bradley used and played rhythm guitar at Buddy Holly's first Decca recording session. His presence allowed Buddy to focus on singing without simultaneously playing guitar. "Grady Martin on rhythm guitar, so Buddy didn't have to sing and play at the same time."

podcast.title: Accidental Invention of the Fuzz Sound (1960)
podcast.body: In late 1960, while playing guitar on Marty Robbins' song "Don't Worry" at Nashville's Quonset Hut studio, Grady Martin accidentally created the first recorded fuzz guitar sound. This occurred when he plugged his six-string baritone guitar directly into a recording console with a faulty transformer in one of its preamps, resulting in a distinct fuzzy sound. Though Marty Robbins initially disliked it, Martin, producer Owen Bradley, and engineer Glenn Snottie recognized its potential, leading to its inclusion in the hit song and subsequently inspiring the development of distortion pedals. "A faulty transformer for one of the preamps inside the console halfway failed, making everything sound all fuzzy."

podcast.title: Design of the First Fuzz Pedal
podcast.body: Following the popularity of the fuzzy guitar sound on Marty Robbins' "Don't Worry," Grady Martin was approached by Gibson Guitars. With assistance from engineer Glenn Snottie and WSM-TV engineer Revis Hobbs, Martin designed a circuit that could replicate this sound on demand. This collaboration led to the creation of the prototype for the first-ever commercial fuzz pedal, the Maestro FZ1 Fuzz tone. "So with some help from Snottie and an engineer from Nashville's WSMTV named Revis Hobbs, Grady designed a circuit that would do just that."

podcast.title: Distinct from Burlison's Style
podcast.body: At the time of the Rock and Roll Trio sessions, Grady Martin's guitar style and effects were distinctly different from Paul Burlison's, highlighting Burlison's unique approach to distorted guitar. "the effect he puts on his guitar is absolutely unlike anything else that you hear from Brady Martin at this point."

podcast.title: Introduced Fuzz Tone to Country Music
podcast.body: Martin later introduced the fuzz tone to country music through his playing on records like Marty Robbins' "Don't Worry," approximately five years after the Rock and Roll Trio's sessions. "Martin did, later, introduce the Fuzz tone to country music, with his playing on records like Marty Robinson's Don't Worry."

podcast.title: Likely Inspired by Paul Burlison's Distortion
podcast.body: The most probable explanation for Grady Martin's later adoption of fuzz tone is that he was inspired by Paul Burlison's intentional use of distorted guitar during the Rock and Roll Trio's Nashville sessions. "the most likely explanation is that Martin was inspired to add Fuzz to his guitar by Paul Burlison."

podcast.title: Nashville A-Team Session Guitarist
podcast.body: Grady Martin was a session guitarist from the Nashville A-Team who added another electric guitar to complement Paul Burlison's on the Rock and Roll Trio's Nashville sessions. "session guitarist Grady Martin added another electric guitar to complement Burlison's."

podcast.title: Session Guitarist on Iconic Recordings
podcast.body: Grady Martin was a prolific session guitarist in Nashville, contributing to hundreds of recordings for prominent artists such as Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, and Buddy Holly. His work as a session musician placed him at the heart of many significant musical developments. "Grady was a session guitarist in Nashville who played on hundreds of recordings for people like Elvis Presley and Johnny Cash and even Buddy Holly."

xref.title: Commercialization of the Fuzz Pedal
xref.body: After hearing the distinctive fuzzy guitar sound on Marty Robbins' "Don't Worry," Gibson Guitars approached Grady Martin to develop a commercial product. Martin, along with Glenn Snottie and Revis Hobbs, designed the circuit, and Gibson manufactured the first-ever fuzz pedal, the Maestro FZ1 Fuzz tone. This product made distortion widely available to guitarists. "When the prototype was ready, Grady and Glenn Snottie took the contraption, which had taken on the form of a foot pedal, to Gibson's offices in Chicago. They took one listen and said, this is brilliant. We'll take it."

xref.title: Use of Distortion Pedal Technology
xref.body: Nirvana is cited as a band that made great use of distortion pedal technology, specifically the Electro-Harmonix Big Muff. This highlights how the accidental invention of the fuzz sound by Grady Martin 30 years earlier continued to influence rock music. "Nirvana making great use of distortion pedal technology invented by accident by Grady Martin, 30 years before that recording session."
